video_title: BlackRock Confirmed Bitcoin Is Here To Stay
gist: Jay Jacobs, BlackRock's US head of equity ETFs, tells Anthony Pompliano that spot Bitcoin ETPs changed Bitcoin's investor mix and volatility without changing its underlying diversifying role, and that in-kind creation demand turned out to be driven by the desire to borrow against and write options on Bitcoin rather than by custody fears. The second half lays out BlackRock's view that AI is now a macro factor rather than a sector theme, that exponential AI demand is colliding with copper, indium and fab supply that takes four to eight years to add, and that the best AI opportunities may sit outside technology in utilities, materials and data-center real estate.

insights.claim: BlackRock's Jay Jacobs argues the biggest measurable impact of spot Bitcoin ETPs was removing digital-asset-exchange onboarding friction, turning Bitcoin into a brokerage-account click for individuals, advisers and institutions, and forcing Bitcoin onto asset-allocation agendas that could previously ignore it.
insights.speaker: Jay Jacobs
insights.so_what: Access, not price forecasting, drove the last flow cycle - watch adviser-platform approvals as the leading indicator of the next tranche of institutional demand.
insights.quote: once the Bitcoin ETPs like IBIT came out, it just made it as easy to access as clicking a button on a brokerage account just like you buy the S&P 500 or buy an individual stock

insights.claim: BlackRock's digital asset strategy is deliberately narrow-and-deep rather than broad-and-many, anchored on the claim that Bitcoin and Ethereum alone are two-thirds to three-quarters of total digital asset market cap, with the firm explicitly ceding long-tail coins to other issuers.
insights.speaker: Jay Jacobs
insights.so_what: Do not expect the largest issuer to chase altcoin ETPs; the open competitive lane for smaller issuers is the long tail, while BlackRock competes on liquidity and structure variants of BTC and ETH.
insights.quote: remember Bitcoin and Ethereum make up anywhere between 2/3 and 3/4 of the whole digital asset market cap

insights.claim: Rather than new coins, BlackRock shipped structural variants - a staked Ethereum ETP (ETHB) alongside an unstaked one, and a Bitcoin premium income product overwriting about 30% of exposure with covered calls - because clients said a zero-coupon asset is hard to fit into cash-flow-driven portfolios.
insights.speaker: Jay Jacobs
insights.so_what: Yield-wrapping is how crypto enters income mandates; expect option-overlay and staking variants, not new underlyings, to be the next product growth vector.
insights.quote: the fact that it's a zero coupon, zero yielding asset um makes it sometimes hard to fit in a portfolio that can be very kind of cash flow based

insights.claim: Bitcoin's volatility has compressed from roughly 80 to roughly 35-40, with competing explanations offered on the show: general Wall Street participation, the ETFs themselves, or the leverage and options layered on top.
insights.speaker: Anthony Pompliano
insights.so_what: A halving of realized vol changes position sizing for vol-targeting and risk-parity allocators, mechanically permitting larger Bitcoin weights at the same risk budget.
insights.quote: It was, you know, 80ish vault asset. Now it's like a 3540 vault asset.

insights.claim: Jacobs attributes the volatility compression to two mechanisms - an ETP options market giving complex trades somewhere to clear, and a larger base of researched long-term holders counterbalancing short-term traders - while declining to claim a single universal cause.
insights.speaker: Jay Jacobs
insights.so_what: If compression is structural market depth rather than a calm-tape artifact, it should survive the next drawdown - a cleanly testable assumption for anyone sizing Bitcoin on historical vol.

insights.claim: The host argues Bitcoin has undergone a 'silent IPO' - ownership transferring from early asymmetric-return holders to a rate-sensitive, higher-correlation investor base - while BlackRock concedes the mix has shifted but insists Bitcoin's fundamental role as a crisis diversifier against stocks and bonds is unchanged.
insights.speaker: Anthony Pompliano and Jay Jacobs
insights.so_what: The largest issuer is still selling Bitcoin as a geopolitical and debasement hedge even as its marginal holder trades off Fed and inflation prints - a positioning that gets tested the next time BTC falls with equities.
insights.quote: So that fundamental diversifying nature of Bitcoin we believe still very much holds uh even as the investor base has maybe shifted over the last few years.

insights.claim: Jacobs expected in-kind creation demand to come from self-custody holders wanting institutional custody after cold-card hack worries, but says the dominant actual driver is financialization - the ability to borrow against Bitcoin once it sits in a wrapper.
insights.speaker: Jay Jacobs
insights.so_what: The wrapper's pull is collateral utility, not safety - implying Bitcoin-backed lending and structured product demand grows faster than pure custody migration.
insights.quote: a bigger piece of it is actually the ability to kind of financialize Bitcoin. Uh borrow against it is a huge use case

insights.claim: The minimum size for an in-kind IBIT transaction has fallen to roughly the $1.5 million level from a substantially higher prior threshold, widening the pool of holders who can swap coins for ETF shares.
insights.speaker: Jay Jacobs
insights.so_what: A lower in-kind minimum is a quiet supply channel from cold storage into regulated wrappers without a taxable sale - visible in creation data if it scales.
insights.quote: right now it's sort of at the $1.5 million level for an inkind transaction. Previously it was much higher than that.

insights.claim: Once Bitcoin is held inside the ETF wrapper, concentrated holders can run protective option strategies, income overlays, or exchange-replication trades that cut Bitcoin risk and add S&P 500 exposure - routes unavailable to raw coin holders.
insights.speaker: Jay Jacobs
insights.so_what: Concentrated crypto wealth now has tax-aware diversification paths, which could mute the forced-selling dynamic that historically accompanied large holders de-risking.

insights.claim: BlackRock has for several months been telling clients that AI adoption now sits alongside GDP growth and interest rates as a primary macro input to market direction, with US price levels levered directly to whether AI accelerates or slows.
insights.speaker: Jay Jacobs
insights.so_what: If the largest asset manager models AI adoption as a macro variable, AI capex guidance is a market-wide risk factor that can only be hedged at index level, not sector level.
insights.quote: if AI slows down the markets will feel it if AI accelerates the markets will enjoy it like it is that important to especially the US markets

insights.claim: BlackRock argues investors misclassify AI as a tech theme when it is equally a healthcare, legal and consumer theme, so allocating to a healthcare fund does not actually reduce AI exposure.
insights.speaker: Jay Jacobs
insights.so_what: Investors rotating into defensives to de-risk from AI may be double-counting the same factor - a reason to measure AI exposure at factor level across the whole book.
insights.quote: Too many people, I think, still view AI as a tech theme.

insights.claim: BlackRock's AI value chain framework spans power companies, data-center real estate, chip manufacturers, data owners, LLM developers, adopting applications and enabling platforms - now dozens of companies globally across many sectors and geographies, not a US large-cap equity play.
insights.speaker: Jay Jacobs
insights.so_what: The value-chain map is a tool for locating where the marginal AI capex dollar lands next rather than repeatedly buying the same crowded US names.

insights.claim: BlackRock believes some of the best AI opportunities currently sit outside technology, in physically constrained materials, utilities and real estate, because software scales at zero incremental cost while compute carries a large physical footprint.
insights.speaker: Jay Jacobs
insights.so_what: An explicit steer from the largest issuer away from crowded semis and hyperscalers toward power, mining and data-center real estate as the better-value claim on the same AI dollar.
insights.quote: And in fact some of the best opportunities we think sort of sit outside of tech right now.

insights.claim: Jacobs identifies the core AI mismatch as exponential demand - LLMs writing their own improvement code around the clock while companies raise token budgets in days or weeks - colliding with a supply side that responds in years.
insights.speaker: Jay Jacobs
insights.so_what: A persistent supply shortfall transfers pricing power to owners of physical bottlenecks rather than model developers - a multi-year relative-value case for hard-asset AI inputs.
insights.quote: So the models are getting much better very quickly. The demand is growing at an exponential rate, but the supply side is lagging by years.

insights.claim: New copper supply needed for data-center buildout and US grid rebuild takes an estimated 4 to 8 years to bring a mine online, making copper a hard constraint on AI infrastructure rather than a cyclical commodity call.
insights.speaker: Jay Jacobs
insights.so_what: Copper lead times cannot compress in response to demand signals, so shortages clear through price - the cleanest expression of AI capex outside of semis.
insights.quote: you could be looking at 4 to 8 years until that copper mine comes online

insights.claim: If photonics and lasers displace copper for in-data-center data transmission, the binding input becomes indium, which is only a small byproduct of zinc mining and processing - a substitution that moves the bottleneck rather than removing it.
insights.speaker: Jay Jacobs
insights.so_what: A non-obvious second-order trade: the copper-substitution narrative leads into a byproduct metal with even less elastic supply than copper itself.

insights.claim: Even with aggressive acceleration and US policy support, new semiconductor fabs take about four years to bring online, capping how fast GPU supply can respond to demand.
insights.speaker: Jay Jacobs
insights.so_what: GPU scarcity is a multi-year condition regardless of announcements, sustaining margins across incumbent chip supply and its memory and packaging adjacencies.
insights.quote: the fabs take about four years to bring online even in the United States

insights.claim: BlackRock screens product ideas on three pillars - does it solve a client need or define an otherwise inaccessible slice of a value chain, does it have positive expected return and portfolio utility, and can a quality ETF actually be built around it - and concludes that AI sub-sub-themes with only a couple of eligible names stop being viable as ETFs.
insights.speaker: Jay Jacobs
insights.so_what: There is a structural floor on how narrow a thematic ETF can go, so the wave of hyper-specific single-component vehicles from smaller issuers carries concentration and liquidity risk the wrapper was not designed for.
insights.quote: when you get really narrow into the sub sub themes of artificial intelligence and there's only a couple of names, it doesn't really resemble an ETF anymore

insights.claim: BlackRock's answer to unpredictable AI rotation is a barbell: one actively managed AI ETF (BAI) run by fundamental manager Tony Kim who rotates across the value chain, plus index-based sleeves for specific bottlenecks - power (PWR), digital infrastructure and data-center real estate (IDGT) and copper mining (ICOP).
insights.speaker: Jay Jacobs
insights.so_what: The sleeve lineup is effectively a published map of where BlackRock expects the AI bottleneck to rotate next - power, digital real estate, copper - with a ready expression for each.

insights.claim: BAI was intentionally designed and distributed as a funding swap out of an investor's existing technology sector allocation, keeping sector and geography exposure roughly neutral while concentrating in the better parts of tech - because the question clients ask most is what to sell, not what to buy.
insights.speaker: Jay Jacobs
insights.so_what: Answering 'what do I sell' is the real distribution unlock for thematic products - a template for judging which new theme funds will actually gather assets.
insights.quote: BAI is designed to be you're selling your tech sector and you're allocating to BAI

themes.theme: ETF structure, tax and liquidity mechanics

insights.claim: There are now more ETFs listed in the US than stocks, this is tracking as a record year for launches, and active ETFs now outnumber index-based ETFs - breadth that Jacobs names as a genuine risk because identically named AI or power ETFs can hold very different portfolios.
insights.speaker: Jay Jacobs
insights.so_what: Selection risk has migrated from picking stocks to picking wrappers - due diligence now means reading holdings and methodology, not the ticker.
insights.quote: there's more ETFs than there are stocks listed in the United States

insights.claim: BlackRock structured its Bitcoin premium income ETF as a 1933 Act product - the structure used for Bitcoin and gold ETFs - rather than the 1940 Act structure behind almost all other ETFs, accepting K-1 complexity in exchange for better after-tax outcomes for investors.
insights.speaker: Jay Jacobs
insights.so_what: Legal structure, not fee or ticker, can drive after-tax return in crypto-income products - a concrete diligence point when comparing superficially identical Bitcoin covered-call funds.

insights.claim: Jacobs pushes back on the blanket assumption that ETFs are inherently the most tax-efficient vehicle, noting that as the wrapper is pushed into more strategies, funds holding options, futures or bonds behave very differently from equity ETFs.
insights.speaker: Jay Jacobs
insights.so_what: The tax-efficiency assumption breaks down precisely in the derivative-heavy products growing fastest - check the underlying instruments before assuming ETF treatment.
insights.quote: it's not as simple as saying ETFs are the most tax efficient vehicle

insights.claim: Jacobs says two ETFs with identical mandates can deliver very different liquidity in stressed markets depending on the breadth and quality of the issuer's market-maker relationships, which BlackRock designs for at construction while deliberately staying out of market making itself.
insights.speaker: Jay Jacobs
insights.so_what: In a liquidity event, spreads and NAV tracking will diverge sharply between same-name ETFs - a reason to prefer vehicles with deep market-maker support even at a higher fee.
insights.quote: I'm going to bet the ETF that has a more robust market making community around it and better relationships is probably going to have a better liquidity experience

insights.claim: BlackRock built systematic rotation ETFs - ingesting hundreds of global data points for buy and sell signals across themes, factors and countries - specifically because clients find selling harder than buying and because doing the same rotation manually realizes capital gains that the ETF structure can defer.
insights.speaker: Jay Jacobs
insights.so_what: Tax-deferred thematic rotation inside a wrapper is a structural edge over running the same trades in a taxable account - directly relevant to any high-turnover theme strategy.

insights.claim: Jacobs' framework for filtering market noise is to ignore daily news and product upgrades and anchor only on identifiable inflection points - a major technology breakthrough, a major regulatory change or a major societal shift - layered on top of a low-cost, tax-efficient, liquid core portfolio.
insights.speaker: Jay Jacobs
insights.so_what: A usable test for deciding when a headline deserves a portfolio change versus when it is noise, especially in fast-moving AI and crypto news cycles.
insights.quote: It's not about the news on a day-to-day basis. It's not about some rumor or some company with necessarily just kind of a new product upgrade. What's changed?

insights.claim: Jacobs identifies ChatGPT's November 2022 launch as the AI inflection point precisely because the underlying model was already a couple of years old and not especially new - the chat interface, not the capability, unlocked mass participation and the fastest-growing online platform ever.
insights.speaker: Jay Jacobs
insights.so_what: Inflection points come from access and interface changes rather than raw capability - the same mechanism Jacobs credits for IBIT and Bitcoin, and a template for spotting the next one.
insights.quote: It was a couple years old already, but they introduced a chat box which meant that so many more people to could participate in it

insights.claim: Jacobs argues part of IBIT's success is that advisers realized the products they discuss with baby boomer clients do not resemble what millennial clients want, forcing advisers to become conversant in Bitcoin to hold both sides of a family relationship through the wealth transfer.
insights.speaker: Jay Jacobs
insights.so_what: Adviser client-retention pressure, rather than adviser conviction in Bitcoin, may be the underappreciated driver of continued IBIT flows during the generational wealth transfer.
insights.quote: the parents saying, you know, talk to me about your large cap growth fund and the kid is saying, tell me about your Bitcoin fund

insights.claim: Data from the host's consumer platform shows its crypto-leaning users hold roughly 20% of assets in primary residence or real estate, only about 10% in crypto, and the bulk in public equities - contradicting the narrative that younger fintech users are overwhelmingly crypto-allocated.
insights.speaker: Anthony Pompliano
insights.so_what: Even in the most crypto-sympathetic retail cohort allocation sits near 10%, a sober anchor for sizing the realistic ceiling on retail crypto flows against the headline narrative.
insights.quote: Only 10% is crypto.
